1.text: Mothballs and cold wool. My grandmother kept her Sunday coats in a closet I hid inside, and I still linger too long in vintage shops because of it.
Diesel and fried bananas together — that's the jeepney stop outside my school in Manila. One whiff and I'm seven again, counting coins for banana cue.
Rain hitting hot pavement. When the monsoon finally broke in Mumbai we'd all run to the balcony, and my mother let the spray soak the laundry anyway.
Garlic hitting hot oil. It meant my dad was home safe from the night shift and frying eggs at six in the morning, humming badly.
Chlorine. I basically lived at the public pool every July, and my mum claimed she could smell my hair from three rooms away.
Sandalwood incense before dawn. My grandfather lit it for morning prayers and I'd pretend to be asleep just to listen to him move around the house.
Two-stroke engine oil. My uncle's fishing boat on the Adriatic — I associate petrol fumes with pure joy, which my wife finds deeply concerning.
Cheap coconut sunscreen melted in a hot glovebox, on the long drive to the coast with all four of us fighting over the middle seat.
Freshly sharpened pencils. New uniform, first day, terrified and thrilled at once. I'm sixty-one now and September still smells like beginnings.
Cardamom pods crushed under the flat of a knife. My grandmother's chai woke the entire Delhi flat at once, no alarm clock required.
Wood smoke in October. Everyone in our Polish village stoked their stoves at dusk, and walking home from school felt like walking into a story.
Corn tortillas puffing on the comal, radio going mid-song. My job was to flip them, my reward was stealing the first one with just salt.
Low tide. Mud, salt, something faintly rotten. Sounds terrible, but that was every dawn at my grandfather's fish stall in Busan, and I loved it.
Cherry pipe tobacco. Nobody smokes a pipe anymore, so when I catch it once a decade on some street corner I have to stop walking for a second.
Mimeograph ink on a warm worksheet. Kids today will never understand why an entire generation of us used to sniff our homework.
Cut grass drifting through a window screen. Saturday cartoons on, my dad wrestling the ancient mower, the whole weekend still unspent.

3.text: Cold wedding leftovers at 2am, on the floor of our first apartment, still in our fancy clothes. Best biryani of my life and it wasn't even warm.
My first dinner after landing in Toronto: instant noodles in a basement apartment, jet-lagged, crying a little, weirdly certain I'd be okay.
A vending machine sandwich in a hospital hallway at 4am, hours after my daughter was born. I have eaten in nice restaurants. None of them compare.
The last New Year dumplings my grandmother folded. She hid a coin in one, I bit it, she laughed until she wheezed. We still make them her way.
Ramen at 2am in a Tokyo alley with my brother, both of us broke, splitting one egg between two bowls and arguing about whose half was bigger.
The camping trip where dad burned everything, including the backup food. We ate crackers and ketchup by the fire and rated it five stars anyway.
Eid dinner during a blackout in Lagos. Candles everywhere, jollof by lantern light, my aunts singing. The power came back and we turned it off.
A fish my grandfather caught that morning, grilled on the beach over driftwood, eaten with our fingers off a newspaper. Salt, lemon, nothing else.
Street tacos on our first date. I dripped salsa down my white shirt within a minute and he laughed so hard I decided to keep him.
Christmas Eve, twelve dishes, my grandmother counting them twice to be sure. I was assigned to guard the pierogi from my cousins and I failed.
Airport noodles with my mother the night I left home for good. Neither of us said much. She kept refilling my cup so she'd have a reason to stay.
My thirtieth birthday on a Cairo rooftop, koshari from downstairs, my friends singing over car horns. Cheap food, priceless view, perfect night.
Trading my boring cheese sandwich for a classmate's kimbap in third grade. First bite of another family's food. I think it made me a cook.
The casseroles after my father's funeral. The whole street cooked for a week. I learned that day that food is how some people say what they can't.
First paycheck, I took my parents to the restaurant they always walked past. My father studied the menu prices in silence, then ordered dessert.
Khichdi during the flood, whole building crammed in one kitchen, water rising outside. Somehow one pot fed thirty people, and nobody went first.

5.text: My carpenter grandfather said measure twice, cut once. Took me thirty years to realize he was never really talking about wood.
Mum used to say you can't read the label from inside the jar. Whenever I'm sure I'm right about myself, I go ask someone standing outside the jar.
Never lend money you can't afford to give away. My uncle said it, then quietly forgave three loans I know of. Probably more.
My aunt said bored is a choice. Infuriating when I was twelve. Now I keep a book in every bag and I've never been stuck anywhere in my life.
Dad taught me to apologize without the word but. He said everything before the but is just a warm-up, and everything after erases it.
Eat first, argue after. My grandmother enforced it at every family fight, and I've watched entire feuds dissolve into soup.
Marry someone you can be bored with. My grandfather said the exciting parts take care of themselves; it's the quiet Tuesdays that need a friend.
Nobody is thinking about you as much as you fear. My uncle told me this before my first speech and it has ruined stage fright for me forever.
Do the dishes tonight, my mother said, because tomorrow-you is family too. I think about that every time I want to leave a mess for later.
Slow is smooth, smooth is fast. Grandpa said it about fixing engines, but it works on emails, arguments, and parallel parking.
Ask the question — the answer is already no if you don't. My mum made me ask for my first job with that line. I got it.
Keep one skill money can't buy. My grandfather meant bread, my father meant welding, I chose listening. All three still hold up.
My sister's rule: cry in the shower, then wash your face and make one decision. Just one. It has carried me through two very bad years.
Show up early and you'll never need to be impressive. Dad drove a delivery truck for forty years and was never once late. People still miss him.
When you drink the water, remember who dug the well. My grandmother said it in Cantonese every time I got too proud of something.
You don't have to attend every argument you're invited to. Dad said this while calmly eating toast during a family row, which proved his point.

7.text: My toddler pointed at a pigeon and shouted chicken with total confidence. He now calls all birds chicken and refuses to be corrected.
Autocorrect changed love you to loathe you in a message to my husband. He replied likewise, darling within four seconds. Married eighteen years.
The cat misjudged the leap to the TV stand, missed entirely, then sat washing herself like the floor was her destination all along.
My grandmother discovered voice messages and now sends me twelve a day, mostly of her narrating what she's cooking. I save every single one.
A colleague joined the budget meeting with a potato filter on and couldn't turn it off. Watching a potato defend quarterly numbers healed me.
Dad texted the family chat: I used to hate facial hair, but then it grew on me. Three of us left the chat. He added us back and sent it again.
I slipped on a grape in the supermarket and somehow turned it into a small lunge, like it was planned. An old man applauded quietly.
My mum tried to type happy birthday in the group chat and the translation app wished my cousin a fortunate explosion. It's her nickname now.
An old photo surfaced of my brother's 2003 frosted tips. He tried to claim it was a different person. In our own kitchen. Wearing his own shirt.
A student wrote that the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell and honestly so am I on an exam. Full marks for the first half, and my heart.
Watched my husband assemble a bookshelf, refuse the manual, finish with nine spare screws, and declare them bonus screws from the factory.
I opened my language app after two weeks away and the owl's disappointment was so theatrical my daughter heard me cackling from the next room.
A seagull stole an entire sausage roll from my father's hand with surgical precision. He speaks of it daily now, like a war veteran.
Showed my son the sitcom I grew up on. He stared blankly for ten minutes, then one joke landed and he laughed exactly like my late father did.
The GPS pronounced my little hometown in Wales so badly that my mother, hearing it over the phone, had to sit down. We replayed it nine times.
My mother-in-law has learned memes but uses them at random. She replied to news of my promotion with a skull. I choose to believe she's proud.

9.text: Grandpa taught me chess by letting me win for a year, then one day stopped. Took me another year to beat him honestly. He framed the scoresheet.
Her hands in the dough, flour to the elbows, and one white fingerprint pressed onto my nose every single time. I'm sixty and I still miss it.
Fishing at dawn with my grandfather, neither of us speaking for hours. I thought we were being quiet for the fish. We were just being quiet.
My parents banned sugar; my grandmother ran a smuggling operation out of her cardigan pockets. Butterscotch, mostly. I never once ratted her out.
Grandfather only told his war stories while weeding, eyes on the soil. I learned to grab a trowel and shut up. I know things my father never heard.
Every afternoon at four we watched her telenovela. She'd translate the drama into Portuguese swearing at the villains. My education, truly.
She answered every letter I ever sent, in handwriting like lace. I still have all of them in a shoebox I can't open more than once a year.
Riding sidesaddle on the back rack of grandpa's bicycle through the rice fields, holding his shirt, absolutely certain nothing could ever go wrong.
Grandma had a superstition for everything. Don't whistle at night, don't sweep after dark. I still put my wallet down carefully because of her.
He fixed radios at the kitchen table and let me hold the solder at seven years old. First time an adult trusted me with something that could burn.
The clatter of mahjong tiles from the next room after midnight, her laugh above all the aunties. I fell asleep to that sound for years.
She sang hymns completely off-key and at full volume while hanging laundry. The neighbors complained once. Only once.
In his orchard he'd pick a tomato, wipe it on his sleeve, salt it from a shaker he kept in his overalls, and hand it over like a sacrament.
Long-distance calls cost a fortune, so grandma shouted her love across the ocean in ninety-second bursts. Efficient woman. I still hear her.
Sunday nights she braided my hair for the school week, tugging exactly twice when I fidgeted. I complained constantly. I'd give a lot for one more.
His coat pocket always held peppermints, lint-covered and ancient. We ate them anyway. All nine grandkids, for thirty years. Same pocket.

11.text: Eat first, decide later. Every crisis in this family has been downgraded to a discussion by the time the rice was done.
We show up. Not always on time, not always dressed right, but at every hospital, graduation, and bad haircut, somebody from us is in the room.
Loud but loyal. The neighbors know our arguments by heart, but let one outsider criticize any of us and watch the whole choir change songs.
Nobody goes to the airport alone. Arrivals or departures, somebody's there with snacks and bad parking. It's how we say the things we don't say.
It'll be funny someday, usually by dinner. We've laughed about the flooded kitchen, the wedding cake disaster, and the goat. Ask about the goat.
Fix it, don't fuss it. Four generations of people who respond to heartbreak with a toolbox. Not always healthy, but the shelves are immaculate.
There's always room for one more chair. My mother fed every stray friend, cousin, and lonely neighbor. The table got longer; so did the family.
Late, but with snacks. We have missed the openings of weddings, movies, and one baptism. No one has ever been hungry while waiting for us.
Ask grandma first. Saves time. Doctors, lawyers, and the internet have all eventually agreed with her, so we cut out the middleman.
We don't whisper. Good news gets shouted, bad news gets shouted, the location of the scissors gets shouted. Secrets don't survive here. It's honest.
Leftovers are love. Nobody leaves this house without a container. My mother once tupperwared soup for a courier who knocked at dinnertime.
Begin anyway. Half this family started over in new countries with wrong papers and three words of the language. Perfect conditions never came.
Same boat, keep rowing. My grandfather said it crossing an actual sea. Now we say it about exams, layoffs, and the group chat's tech problems.
If in doubt, put the kettle on. Illness, breakups, spiders in the bath — this family has no problem that gets discussed without tea in hand.
Argue at full volume, forgive by breakfast. We've never mastered the cold shoulder. Someone always cracks and asks who wants eggs.
Keep the receipts, tell the stories. Half our inheritance is paperwork, the other half is legends. Both get pulled out at every gathering.

13.text: The first coffee before anyone else wakes up. Fifteen minutes of steam and silence before the house needs me. It's basically a spa.
The bus driver saw me running and actually waited. Whole day went differently because one stranger touched the brake for three seconds.
My eight-year-old still reaches for my hand at the crossing without looking up. I know the clock is running on that. Today it happened twice.
The radiator works. Cold snap outside, socks drying on it, whole flat smelling like warm laundry. Some winters taught me not to skip this one.
A rambling three-minute voice note from my mum about nothing — the market, a rude pigeon, her knee. She's eighty-two. Nothing is my favorite topic.
The balcony tomatoes finally turned red after I threatened them for weeks. Ate one standing up in the sun like it was an award ceremony.
Left my wallet on a bench in the park. A teenager chased me two blocks to return it, then acted like I was weird for trying to thank him.
Walked up all four flights and my knees said nothing. At seventy-three, a silent staircase is a standing ovation.
Real rain, finally, after two dry months. I stood in the doorway with my father just smelling it. The farmers group chat was pure celebration.
My daughter texted first. No occasion, no request, just a photo of a dog she saw. Parents of teenagers will understand the size of this.
The quiet hour after night shift when the streets are empty and the bakery is just opening. Warm bread on the walk home. Nurses know.
A song from my university days came on the radio in a taxi and the driver turned it up without me asking. We both sang. Terribly.
My neighbor left flatbread on my door handle again, still warm, no note. Third year running. We've never discussed it. That's the beauty.
The grandkids stayed on the video call a whole hour and even fought over who got to hold the phone. Fought over me! I've still got it.
Fresh sheets, laundry dried outside in actual wind. Climbing into that bed tonight will be the closing ceremony of a perfectly ordinary day.
The power stayed on through the whole dinner rush. Every plate went out hot. Small restaurant, small mercy, huge difference.

15.text: Apparently at four I called my teacher mum in front of the entire class, then doubled down and asked her what was for dinner. It's been forty years.
I ate the decorative wax pear at my aunt's house and, when caught, complimented the cooking. My cousins present it at every gathering like evidence.
I fell asleep face-first in the cake at my own fifth birthday party. There are photos. There is, tragically, also video, digitized twice now.
Age six, I followed the ice cream truck four blocks like a tiny detective. Half the neighborhood searched for me. I came back with a cone, unbothered.
I opened a shop on the porch selling my parents' belongings at excellent prices. Dad bought back his own radio for fifty cents. He kept the receipt.
At my uncle's wedding I grabbed the microphone and announced my sister had just lost a tooth. The band played a fanfare. She still hasn't forgiven me.
I wheeled the wrong suitcase off the carousel in Frankfurt and didn't notice for two days. A very patient stranger got his shirts back ironed.
The dog was white. I had watercolors. For one afternoon he was a rainbow, and the family has never allowed me to live down my masterpiece.
I ran away from home at seven, meaning I sat at the end of the driveway with a packed lunch until it got dark and dinner smelled too good.
I called the emergency line because my brother wouldn't share the remote. The operator asked to speak to my mother. So did I, apparently, sobbing.
Every formal family portrait from 1998 features me mid-sneeze. The photographer offered a retake. My grandmother said no, that's just how he looks.
I locked everyone out during my cousin's birthday and ate a quarter of the cake alone before they got a window open. I showed no remorse. Still don't.
In a dead-silent church I asked my grandmother, at full volume, if she was older than God. The priest had to pause. She answered nearly, keep praying.
I wore red rain boots every day for a year, including to a wedding and to the beach. In every photo from 1996, there they are. No regrets.
At my own baptism I grabbed the priest's glasses and threw them into the font. My grandmother called it my first act of independence, proudly.
First week as an exchange student I rode the bus the wrong way for an hour, too shy to ask, and ended up at the sea. I sat down and enjoyed the view.

17.text: The cupboard under my grandmother's stairs, between the pickle jars and winter boots. Smelled of vinegar and dust. Best office I've ever had.
The gap behind the sofa where the curtain pooled. I was invisible there, except for being a sofa-shaped lump that giggled.
Halfway up the guava tree behind our house in Nairobi. Snacks provided by the venue. My mother knew exactly where I was and let me believe otherwise.
The attic above the rice store, up a ladder I wasn't allowed on. Warm sacks, dust in the light beams, and the whole market talking below me.
The back seat of dad's parked car with a blanket and a library book. Not hidden from anyone, exactly. Just unavailable for chores.
My grandmother's wardrobe, deep in the coats. I read the right book far too young and spent two winters checking the back for snow.
Behind the living room curtains, feet in full view. I was five and believed I'd cracked it. My family performed twenty minutes of confusion nightly.
Under my bed with a torch, comics, and biscuits, listening to my sisters hunt for me. Sometimes I'd fall asleep and cause a genuine panic.
The flat roof by the water tank. All of Tehran humming below, pigeons for company, and nobody thought to look up. My first real thinking spot.
The hollow inside the neighbor's hedge, entrance known to exactly three children. We held elections in there. I was briefly a president.
The big laundry basket, under a strategic layer of towels. Undefeated for two full years until I grew and my knees betrayed me.
Under the church pews after Sunday service in São Paulo while the adults talked forever. Cool stone floor, forest of legs, holy quiet.
The footwell under my father's desk while he did paperwork. He'd slide biscuits down without ever stopping writing. Neither of us said a word.
The hayloft with the missing ladder rung that scared the other kids off. Just me, the swallows, and the whole farm going about its business below.
The bathtub, curtain drawn, cushions installed. My mother found my reading nest weekly and dismantled it weekly. We were both very stubborn.
Behind the tomato pots on our Athens balcony, knees to my chin, watching the street through the railing like a tiny inspector. Nobody rushed me.

19.text: Bus driver. Specifically the number 12. I practiced the door lever motion on the fridge handle for a full year. The dream had detail.
Marine biologist, by which I meant a person who hugs dolphins professionally. Nobody warned me about the statistics requirements.
A priest, then an astronaut, then a priest astronaut. My grandmother saw no conflict and said space needed blessing too. She backed all my plans.
A shopkeeper. I lined up tins in the pantry, priced them with stickers, and made my family queue. In fairness, I now run a shop. Manifested it.
A cartoonist. I filled the margins of every schoolbook with a duck detective. My maths teacher kept one page. She told me at my graduation.
A teacher. I ran a strict classroom for my little brothers with homework and a bell. Both hated it. Both showed up. I've been teaching 26 years now.
Truck driver, entirely because they pulled the horn when we pumped our arms from the back seat. Eight-year-old me valued applause on demand.
A ballerina and a wrestler, simultaneously, in the same outfit. I want to find that kid and tell her that's basically what adult life became.
Official ice cream taster. I'd read somewhere the job existed and told everyone with the confidence of a boy who had already been hired.
A doctor, because my grandmother announced it to the whole village when I was eight. I became one at 26, mostly because arguing with her was futile.
Striker for Boca Juniors. I had the number picked, the goal celebration choreographed, the interviews rehearsed in the mirror. The talent, less so.
An archaeologist, which to eight-year-old me meant dinosaur bones and treasure. I'm an accountant now, but I still dig through old things all day.
An inventor. I kept a notebook of designs: a homework machine, a dog translator, an endless biscuit. Honestly, the market is still waiting on all three.
A flight attendant, because they were the only people I knew who had actually seen the sky from inside. I grew up to fly anyway, just in economy.
A farmer like my grandfather, with his exact hat. I got the hat when he passed. The farm went to my uncle, but the hat was always the real inheritance.
A pop star. Hairbrush microphone, bedroom mirror, full choreography to an audience of stuffed animals. Frankly, my best performances to date.
